title: Reducing QUBO Complexity in Drone Delivery Through Classical Feasibility Preprocessing
authors: Silvie Illésová, Vojtěch Novák, Martin Beseda
abstract: Drone-delivery planning combines routing decisions with operational constraints such as payload capacity and limited onboard energy, resulting in combinatorial optimization problems that can become costly to encode directly in binary form. This work investigates a hybrid quantum--classical approach in which candidate drone missions are generated and evaluated classically before constructing a quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) model for mission selection. Payload- and energy-infeasible missions are removed during preprocessing, while the reduced QUBO is solved using exact enumeration, simulated annealing (SA), and the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA), with mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) used as a classical reference. Experiments on controlled synthetic delivery instances evaluate solution quality, the effect of preprocessing, and computational scaling. Exact QUBO optimization reproduces the MILP optimum on the evaluated small instances, while SA achieves $100\%$ feasibility with a median optimality gap of $0\%$. Combined payload-and-energy preprocessing reduces the mean number of QUBO variables by $29.60\%$ and quadratic interactions by $49.20\%$, while reducing mean SA runtime by $31.26\%$. In contrast, the evaluated shallow statevector-based QAOA configuration achieves lower feasibility and is restricted to small QUBO instances. These results indicate that, in the considered setting, the main practical benefit of the hybrid architecture comes from classical feasibility preprocessing that reduces the binary search space before QUBO-based optimization.
summary: This paper tackles drone delivery planning, a complex optimization problem, by proposing a hybrid quantum-classical solution. It uses classical preprocessing to filter out physically impossible routes, drastically reducing the size of the resulting QUBO model. The results show that this classical filtering step provides the most significant practical advantage, improving the performance of quantum solvers like SA.
main_problem: The paper addresses the complex combinatorial optimization problem of drone delivery planning, which involves routing decisions subject to operational constraints like payload capacity and limited energy.
main_result: The primary benefit of the hybrid quantum-classical approach is found in classical feasibility preprocessing, which significantly reduces the size of the QUBO search space and improves the performance of subsequent quantum optimization methods like SA.
method: A hybrid quantum-classical methodology is employed: classical preprocessing filters out infeasible mission candidates, reducing the problem to a smaller QUBO model solved by exact enumeration, Simulated Annealing (SA), or QAOA.
model_or_system: The system models drone delivery missions involving a set of customers, formulated as a QUBO optimization problem. Constraints include payload capacity and total energy consumption, which are handled via preprocessing or penalty terms.
key_observables: Solution quality (feasibility, optimality gap), reduction in QUBO variables and quadratic interactions, and computational runtime.
important_parameters: Maximum payload capacity ($W_{	ext{max}}$), available energy capacity ($E_{	ext{max}}$), and the size of the problem instance ($n$).
main_assumptions: The main assumption is that separating deterministic feasibility checks (classical) from the combinatorial selection (QUBO) yields practical benefits. Limitations include using synthetic instances and restricting QAOA to shallow statevector simulations.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem, details the hybrid methodology (classical preprocessing followed by QUBO solving), presents results comparing various solvers (MILP, SA, QAOA), and concludes by emphasizing the role of preprocessing in complexity reduction.
why_interesting: While the core application is logistics, the methodology involves mapping a constrained combinatorial problem onto a QUBO framework and analyzing the computational benefit of classical filtering before applying quantum optimization techniques, which is relevant to quantum algorithm design.

Customers are generated within a 10×10 km service region around a central depot and are associated with package weights. Candidate missions start and end at the depot and contain at most three customer stops. Colors and line styles distinguish the example missions, while payload and energy feasibility are evaluated before construction of the QUBO.
